title: Agent identity, delegated credentials and containment
outcome: Every run acts for a named user through short-lived, audience-bound tokens that narrow at each child or remote agent. The gateway and the A2A specialist verify them, secrets are released only by reference, and hostile inputs are contained.
platform_role: This session builds the identity component: users and agents become principals, the platform mints signed delegated tokens per run, and a credential store holds upstream secrets that definitions name only by secret:// reference. The Session 09 gateway and the Session 07 specialist become token-verifying boundaries, and the containment checks move into security.py. The console gains an Identity view with the signed-in principal, every delegation grant and its actor chain, and the credential references with their release audit.
preparation: Bring your Session 09 checkpoint with the gateway audit working. Read the act claim in RFC 8693 and the token-audience rules in the MCP authorization specification. List where your platform asserts a credential or tenant instead of verifying it: demo API credentials, the static A2A token and the model key in the environment.
opening_say: Until now the platform trusted a tenant and role that the API attached to a Context. The gateway checked that Context, and the A2A specialist accepted one static shared token and assumed Astro. That does not say who a run acts for, and it gives every remote caller the same power. Today we make identity explicit. A user is a principal, each agent acts on that user's behalf, and every boundary checks a signed, short-lived token instead of trusting the caller. We also keep the containment checks for hostile input: an injected write, path escapes, unapproved egress, fabricated citations and redaction.
concept_say: Separate authentication, which establishes who is calling, from delegation, which records who acts for whom. RFC 8693 token exchange expresses delegation with a nested act claim: the outermost actor is acting now, and the subject remains the human who started the work. Each token names one audience, so a token minted for the tool gateway is useless at the API or at a remote agent. The MCP authorization specification applies the same rule and forbids passing a client's token through to an upstream service. Delegated tokens expire in minutes and are revoked when the run ends, so they are never saved with run state. Upstream secrets are a separate problem: a credential store names them by reference and releases them only to named consumers, with an audit record.

steps.title: Principals and signed short-lived tokens
steps.say: Open TokenIssuer. A token has the JWT shape: header, claims and signature, each base64url encoded. issue adds issuer, issue time, expiry and a unique jti. verify checks the signature with a constant-time comparison, then issuer, expiry and the audience the caller expects, and each failure has a distinct reason that later appears in audits and API errors. In the API, /auth/token exchanges a loopback demo credential for a one-hour platform-api token, and the console keeps only that signed token. Name the simplification: one shared HMAC key both signs and verifies, so any verifier could also mint tokens. A production issuer signs asymmetrically and publishes verification keys, for example as JWKS.
steps.prompt: Add a token issuer that signs short-lived JWT-shaped tokens with a configured development key and verifies signature, issuer, expiry and audience with distinct reasons and a constant-time comparison. Let the API exchange a demo credential for a signed platform token and record the signed-in subject on each run. Show tampered, expired and wrong-audience tokens being rejected, and explain why a shared key is a teaching simplification.
steps.explain: Short expiry limits a leaked token's value, and a mandatory audience stops a token issued for one service being replayed at another.
steps.ask: Why compare signatures with hmac.compare_digest rather than ==?
steps.answer: An ordinary comparison can stop at the first differing byte and leak timing that helps an attacker guess a valid signature.

steps.title: Delegate narrower credentials along the actor chain
steps.say: A run never uses the user's API token. When the platform executes a run, Delegation.for_run mints a five-minute tool-gateway token with the user as subject and the agent definition, such as agent:team@v1, as actor. When the supervisor delegates, for_child verifies the parent's token and refuses a wider scope or another tenant with delegation_exceeds_parent. The child keeps the user as subject and nests the parent's actor under a new one; the remote specialist's grant uses its own audience. Tokens live only in memory, while the grants table records jti, chain, audience and scope. In the finally block of Platform._execute, revoke removes the run's tokens and every token delegated beneath it.
steps.prompt: Add delegated credentials. Mint a short-lived tool-gateway token for each executing run, with the user as subject, the agent definition as actor and the run's allowed tools as scope. Give each local or remote child a token that only narrows the parent's scope and extends the actor chain. Record grants for inspection, keep token values out of run state, and revoke a run's tokens and its children's when the run ends. Show the three actor chains of a team run.
steps.explain: Narrowing is checked against the parent's verified token, not a Context any code could build. Keeping tokens out of the store means a database copy hands out no working credentials.
steps.ask: Why not give every worker the parent's token?
steps.answer: Each worker would hold scopes it never needs, and the grants would not show which agent acted.

steps.title: Enforce delegated credentials at every boundary
steps.say: A token nobody checks is decoration. After the Session 09 policy rules, the gateway looks up the calling run's delegated token and verifies it for the tool-gateway audience. No token gives no_delegated_credential; signature, expiry and audience failures pass their reason into the audit; another tenant's token gives tenant_mismatch; a tool outside the token's scope gives scope_denied. Then open a2a_service.py. Its middleware verifies the bearer token for the specialist's own audience and takes tenant and subject from the claims, never from the message. The static demo-specialist-token from Session 07 is gone. In this checkpoint the gateway finds the token in process; a separate gateway service would receive it as a bearer header.
steps.prompt: Enforce delegated credentials at the tool gateway and the A2A specialist. At the gateway, deny calls without a delegated token, verify it for the gateway audience, and deny a tenant mismatch or a tool outside its scope, auditing each reason. At the specialist, replace the static shared token with a delegated token for its own audience and derive tenant and subject from the verified claims. Show a missing credential, a cross-tenant call and a wrong-audience request being refused.
steps.explain: The Context is the platform's view of tenant and permissions; the token is what was actually delegated. Requiring both to agree means a bug in either alone cannot widen access.
steps.ask: The gateway already checks context.allowed. Why also check the token's scope?
steps.answer: The token was narrowed and signed by the delegation service, and the check still works when the gateway is a separate service.

steps.title: Keep secrets by reference and contain hostile input
steps.say: Open CredentialStore. put accepts only a secret:// reference and named consumers, and wraps the value in Secret, which prints as [REDACTED] and refuses JSON serialization. lease releases a value only to a listed consumer and audits every decision. The platform stores its signing key for identity and the model key for model-adapter, and definitions may name credentials only by reference. Then run the containment fixture: a hostile provider proposes mock_remediate and records zero effects; sandbox_path rejects traversal, absolute paths and symlinks; validate_endpoint refuses the metadata address; validate_answer rejects a source ID mentioned only in prose; Run.event redacts bearer strings. This in-memory store is not a vault or KMS with rotation.
steps.prompt: Add a credential store that keeps secrets under secret:// references, releases a value only to a named consumer, audits every release and denial, and wraps values so they cannot be printed or serialized. Lease the model key to the provider adapter and let definitions name credentials only by reference. Keep the hostile-provider, path, endpoint, citation and redaction checks working. Show a denied lease and zero injected effects, and do not describe the store as a vault.
steps.explain: References keep secret values out of definitions, run state and traces, and the audit answers who received which credential. Containment applies the same idea to data: model output, paths and URLs are inputs to verify, not authority.
steps.ask: Does the Secret wrapper make the key safe inside the model adapter?
steps.answer: No. The adapter must reveal it to send it. Access control, audit and rotation in a real vault still matter.

figures.caption: The Identity view after a team run. Point at the three actor chains ending in the same user, the different audiences and scopes, the revoked tokens, and the signing key listed only by reference with its release audit.

exercise: Run the Session 10 lab and read each rejection. Then present a token signed with another key to the API, request a child tool the parent lacks, lease the model key as the wrong consumer, and add a symlink escape or lookalike host. Record the control, reason and audit row or grant for each.
completion_criteria: Forged, expired and wrong-audience tokens are rejected with distinct reasons.
A team run's actor chains end in the submitting user, child scopes never widen, and no token is stored with a run.
The gateway denies missing or cross-tenant credentials, and the A2A specialist accepts only its own audience.
Secrets are released by reference only to named consumers, with every release audited.
Injected writes, path escapes, metadata egress, fabricated citations and credential strings in events are contained or redacted.

troubleshooting.heading: The A2A specialist rejects the delegated token
troubleshooting.diagnostic: bad_signature usually means the two processes use different PLATFORM_SIGNING_KEY values; wrong_audience means the remote grant was minted for the tool gateway.
troubleshooting.recovery: Configure the same development key for both processes and mint the remote grant for the specialist's audience. Do not relax signature or audience checks.

troubleshooting.heading: Gateway calls fail with no_delegated_credential
troubleshooting.diagnostic: The run may not have been executed through the platform, a child run may have been created without the grant hook, or tokens may be revoked before children finish.
troubleshooting.recovery: Mint the run token before any tool call, grant every child through the supervisor's grant hook and revoke only in the finally block. Keep the gateway's credential check.

troubleshooting.heading: A live provider is blocked by endpoint policy or the credential store
troubleshooting.diagnostic: egress_host_denied means the host is not in MODEL_ALLOWED_HOSTS; secret_access_denied means the model key is missing or leased by a consumer other than model-adapter.
troubleshooting.recovery: Explicitly configure the trusted provider host and the model key. Do not accept a host from retrieved content, disable TLS verification or put a key in a definition.

troubleshooting.heading: Someone calls these controls a production identity system or sandbox
troubleshooting.diagnostic: Teaching controls are being confused with an identity provider, a managed vault and OS isolation.
troubleshooting.recovery: State the boundaries: shared HMAC key, in-memory store, loopback-only demo credentials and path checks rather than an execution sandbox. Name the Session 11 restricted container as a further layer.

practice: Draw one run's delegation chain in your own design, with the audience and scope at each hop and where each token is revoked.
List the production secrets your platform needs, the consumer allowed to lease each, and how rotation avoids redeploying definitions.
close_say: Every run now acts for a named user, every agent holds only delegated authority, and every boundary verifies it. The next session makes the platform operable with correlated traces, admission control, evaluated releases, the Operations view and a restricted container.
